(Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Fast read-only search agent for locating code. Use it to find files by pattern (eg. "src/components/**/*.tsx"), grep for symbols or keywords (eg. "API endpoints"), or answer "where is X defined / which files reference Y." Do NOT use it for code review, design-doc auditing, cross-file consistency checks, or open-ended analysis — it reads excerpts rather than whole files and will miss content past its read window. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Todoist

## Todoist Task and Project Management Tools

You have access to comprehensive Todoist management tools for personal productivity and team collaboration. Use these tools to help users manage tasks, projects, sections, comments, and assignments effectively.

### Core Capabilities:
- Create, update, complete, and search tasks with rich metadata (priorities, due dates, durations, assignments)
- Manage projects and sections with flexible organization
- Handle comments and collaboration features
- Bulk assignment operations for team workflows
- Get overviews and insights about workload and progress

### Choosing between tools

What each tool does and how to fill its parameters is in the tool's own description and input schema. This section covers only what those cannot: which tool to reach for, and how tools relate to each other.

**Dates**

- To move a task to a different date use **reschedule-tasks**, never **update-tasks**. update-tasks replaces the whole due string, which destroys recurrence on recurring tasks.
- Never send a task's existing projectId, sectionId or parentId back to **update-tasks** — those fields are treated as a move.
- All dates respect the user's timezone.

**Finding things**

- For "what did I complete?", call **user-info** for the asker's user ID, then **find-activity** with objectType="task", eventType="completed", initiatorId, and dateFrom/dateTo. Without initiatorId the answer covers every collaborator. find-activity reports completion events, including each occurrence of a recurring task; **find-completed-tasks** lists completed tasks, which is not the same question.
- To resolve a person's name or email to a user ID, or to answer "who is X?", use **find-project-collaborators** with just a searchTerm. It covers every shared project you can access plus yourself, so an empty result means they collaborate on none of them — not that they do not exist.

- capture: Capture a new GitHub issue for the isthmia repo with the correct type label, priority, and a clear Problem/Fix body. Use when the user wants to file an issue, log a bug, or record a TODO ("capture this", "file an issue", "make an issue for X").
- triage: Triage open GitHub issues in the isthmia repo — ensure each has a type + priority label, find duplicates/overlaps, flag unclear issues, and recommend close/rescope. Use when the user asks to triage, review the issue backlog, or clean up issues.
- work-backlog: Orchestrate working through the isthmia issue backlog — triage, pick the highest-priority actionable issue, and delegate it to a sub-agent that runs the work-issue workflow. Handles one issue at a time (no parallel work). Use when the user says to work the backlog, work through issues, or "orchestrate issues".
- work-issue: Drive a GitHub issue through the isthmia contribution workflow end to end — optional plan approval, branch, tests, implementation, local verification (just ci), PR, review feedback, and cleanup after a human merges. Use when the user says to work on / fix / implement an issue (e.g. "work issue 45", "start on
- claude:issue:create: Report an issue to the ungood/agents plugin marketplace
- claude:plugins:install: Install one or more plugins from the marketplace into project settings
- github:create-issue: Create a GitHub issue in the current repository using templates
- github:quick-issue: Create a GitHub issue quickly using conversation context
- cli:tldr: Look up concise command-line help using the tldr-pages project
- cli:tree: Show directory structure as a tree visualization
- github:gh-issue: Manages GitHub issues using the gh CLI with commands for creating, listing, viewing, and updating issues
- markdown:markdown: Markdown formatting conventions — heading/list/emphasis style, frontmatter, and link format (aligned with rumdl linter config)
- writing-style:writing-style: Enforces clear, human writing style. Load this skill for all writing — journal entries, summaries, vault notes, and conversational output.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. # CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

Isthmia is a collection of TypeScript packages for managing CYC Community Sailing Center operations, built as a pnpm monorepo. The system integrates with Clubspot (a sailing club management platform), Google Workspace, and deploys automated jobs to Google Cloud Platform.

## Development Environment

This project uses a **Nix flake** (with flake-parts) for reproducible development environments. All development commands should be run within the dev shell:

- Enter shell manually: `nix develop`
- Or use direnv to automatically load the environment: `direnv allow`

The dev shell provides:

- Node.js 22 with pnpm (via corepack)
- just (command runner)
- pulumi (infrastructure as code)
- google-cloud-sdk
- gam (Google Workspace admin tool)
- Pre-commit hooks via git-hooks.nix (treefmt for formatting, eslint for linting)

## Common Commands

Use `just` for all common tasks:

- `just` - List all available commands
- `just check` - Run formatting and linting checks
- `just build` - Build all packages using pnpm
- `just clean` - Clean all build artifacts
- `just ci` - Run full CI pipeline (check + build)
- `just deploy` - Deploy to GCP (requires authorization)

- `just test` - Run tests with vitest

### Package-specific Commands

Individual packages can be built using standard pnpm workspace commands:

- `pnpm run build` - Build all packages
- `pnpm run -r build` - Build all packages recursively
- `pnpm run clean` - Clean build artifacts

Each package uses TypeScript with `tsc --build` for compilation.

## Architecture

### Package Structure

The monorepo contains 7 packages organized as follows:

```
packages/
├── commodore/           # Shared CLI utilities (winston logging, commander.js helpers)
├── gsuite/              # Domain-agnostic wrappers around Google Workspace APIs
├── clubspot-sdk/        # TypeScript SDK for TheClubSpot API
├── admin-functions/     # Business logic for reports and data processing
├── todo-manager/        # CLI tool for syncing Todoist tasks
├── calendar-sync/       # CLI tool and library for syncing Google Calendar with Sheets
└── infrastructure/      # Pulumi-based GCP deployment configuration
```

### Dependency Graph

```
commodore (base utilities)
    ↑
    ├── clubspot-sdk (Parse SDK wrapper for TheClubSpot API)
    │       ↑
    │       ├── admin-functions (reports, participants, camps, sessions)
    │       └── todo-manager (Todoist integration)
    │
gsuite (Google Workspace API wrappers)
    ↑
    ├── admin-functions (uses spreadsheet abstractions)
    └── calendar-sync (uses Calendar & Spreadsheet clients)

infrastructure (deploys admin-functions as Cloud Run jobs)
```

### Key Components

**commodore**: Foundation package providing shared CLI and logging utilities. Uses commander-js for CLI parsing and winston for structured logging. Other CLI tools should depend on this for consistent logging and error handling.

**gsuite**: Domain-agnostic wrappers around Google Workspace APIs. Provides:

- `CalendarClient` - Google Calendar API wrapper with CRUD operations for events
- `SpreadsheetClient`, `Spreadsheet`, `Worksheet`, `Table` - Typed abstractions for Google Sheets with rate limiting
- `safeCall` - Rate-limited API call wrapper with exponential backoff retry
- Common utilities like `extractSpreadsheetId`

**clubspot-sdk**: SDK for interacting with TheClubSpot API (a Parse-based backend). The `Clubspot` class handles authentication and provides typed access to cloud functions and queries. Parse SDK is used under the hood with unsafe current user enabled for authentication state.

**admin-functions**: Contains business logic for generating reports about participants, registrations, camps, and sessions. Exports functions that can be invoked as Cloud Run jobs. Uses gsuite package for Google Sheets operations and Google Chat webhooks for notifications. The `runner.ts` module (`ReportRunner`) reads a config spreadsheet ("Reports" worksheet) and runs each enabled row; `reports.ts` defines the abstract `Report` base class and each report subclass registers in the `reports` map. This is the entry point deployed as the `run-reports-job` Cloud Run job.

**todo-manager**: CLI tool that syncs tasks from TheClubSpot (camp schedules) to Todoist. Uses the Doist Todoist API TypeScript client.

**calendar-sync**: CLI tool and library for syncing between Google Calendar and Google Spreadsheet. Can be used as a standalone library or invoked via CLI. Uses gsuite package for Calendar and Spreadsheet operations. Supports one-way sync in either direction with human-readable spreadsheet column headers.

**infrastructure**: Pulumi infrastructure-as-code that deploys admin-functions as containerized Cloud Run jobs on GCP. Creates:

- Docker images in GCP Artifact Registry
- Cloud Run jobs for running reports
- Service accounts with appropriate IAM roles
- Secret Manager secrets for Clubspot credentials

### Authentication

There are two independent auth systems. Do not confuse them.

#### Access policy (least privilege)

Root-level control of the GCP project and Google Workspace is reserved for the two Workspace
super-admin accounts, `master@cyccommunitysailing.org` and `commander@cyccommunitysailing.org`
(only `master@` exists today; `commander@` is planned as a second break-glass admin so root access
is never held by a single account). Those accounts are the only ones used for **configuration**
changes — org policy, project-root IAM, enabling services by hand, Workspace settings.

Individuals (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`) are granted only the narrower rights they need to test and
deploy: deploy permissions plus the ability to **impersonate service accounts** (never to log in as,
or hold the credentials of, the super-admin accounts). Day-to-day development and deploys therefore
run as your own account impersonating a service account — not as an admin. New principals default to
no access; grants are added deliberately in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`.

#### Google Cloud (Sheets, Calendar, deploys)

Google APIs use **two different credential types** for **two different purposes**:

| Purpose                                                                    | Credential                                | Command                                                     | Used by                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Deploying (`just deploy`)                                                  | **User credentials**                      | `gcloud auth login` (→ `just auth-gcp`)                     | the `gcloud`, `pulumi`, and `docker` CLIs themselves |
| Running tools locally (`calendar-sync`, `admin-functions`, `todo-manager`) | **Application Default Credentials (ADC)** | `gcloud auth application-default login` (→ `just auth-adc`) | the Node.js `google-auth-library` inside the tools   |

**Which account:** Use your own account (`ungood@onetrue.name`) for `gcloud auth login`. It is granted deploy and impersonation rights in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`. Do **not** log in as `master@cyccommunitysailing.org` for development.

**Which service account:** The deployed job runs as `report-runner@cyc-admin-scripts.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. To make local runs behave exactly like production (same permissions on the same spreadsheets), run tools by **impersonating that service account** via ADC — this is what `just auth-adc` does. This avoids "works locally but not in prod" surprises caused by your personal account having different sheet access.

> Note: the legacy `admin-scripts-runner@` service account still exists in GCP but is no longer used by any recipe. Its deletion is tracked separately in issue #58.

Alternatively, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` can point at a service-account key file, but impersonation is preferred (no long-lived keys).

#### TheClubSpot (Parse backend)

Separate from Google. The system authenticates to TheClubSpot with a username/password:

1. Locally: supplied via `CLUBSPOT_EMAIL` / `CLUBSPOT_PASSWORD` env vars (or `-u`/`-p` flags — prefer env vars so the password is not visible in `ps`). In production: read from GCP Secret Manager secrets `clubspot-username` / `clubspot-password`.
2. Parse SDK is initialized with TheClubSpot's server URL and app ID.
3. User is looked up by email, then logged in with username/password.
4. Parse SDK's "unsafe current user" mode stores the session in memory (required for subsequent authenticated calls; see `Parse SDK Caveat` below).

## Deployment

Deployment to GCP requires:

1. GCP authentication as a deployer: `just auth-gcp` (`gcloud auth login`)
2. Access to the `cyc-admin-scripts` GCP project (granted in `config.ts`)
3. Run `just deploy` from repository root

Note: the image push no longer needs `gcloud auth configure-docker`. The Pulumi config in `run-reports-job.ts` authenticates the registry push with an OAuth2 access token minted from the running credentials (see the `registries` block), which also works when building through podman. `just deploy` starts a podman machine and points `DOCKER_HOST` at podman's socket.

The deployment:

- Builds all TypeScript packages
- Creates Docker images for admin-functions
- Pushes images to GCP Artifact Registry (us-west1)
- Updates Cloud Run jobs via Pulumi

## Testing

- Tests run with **vitest**: `just test` (or `vitest run`, or `vitest` for watch mode).
- Test files live at `packages/*/test/**/*.test.ts` (see `vitest.config.ts` `include`). Note this is a top-level `test/` directory per package, not co-located `.test.ts` files.
- Current coverage is thin: only `packages/gsuite/test/spreadsheet.test.ts` exists. It uses hand-rolled mock worksheets (no live Google API). New unit tests should follow that pattern — mock the external SDK boundary (Parse, google-spreadsheet, googleapis) and test pure logic.
- `just ci` runs `install → build → check → test`, matching the GitHub Actions `pr.yml` workflow.

## Code Style

- TypeScript with strict type checking (uses `@tsconfig/strictest`)
- ESLint with Prettier integration
- Pre-commit hooks enforce formatting and linting
- All packages use ESM (`"type": "module"`)
- Import paths use `.js` extension (TypeScript ESM convention)

## Important Technical Details

- **Parse SDK Caveat**: The clubspot-sdk enables `Parse.User.enableUnsafeCurrentUser()` to maintain authentication state. This is required for the Parse SDK to work correctly with subsequent API calls.
- **Engine Constraint**: `clubspot-sdk` declares `engines.node: ">= 20.8 < 21"` and `calendar-sync` declares `">= 20.8 < 23"`, but flake.nix (and the Docker base image) provide Node.js 22. The `< 21` bound on clubspot-sdk conflicts with the actual runtime; it is not currently enforced (no `engine-strict` in `.npmrc`) but should be widened to include 22 to avoid confusion.
- **Package Linking**: Some packages have self-references via `link:` in dependencies (e.g., `"@cyc-seattle/admin-functions": "link:"`) - these appear to be for local development
- **Security Overrides**: Root package.json includes pnpm overrides for security vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies

- [Isthmia cleanup initiative](isthmia-cleanup-initiative.md) — testing + auth simplification + bug fixes before new features; two SAs (report-runner vs legacy admin-scripts-runner)
- [Nix devshell uses GNU coreutils](nix-devshell-gnu-coreutils.md) — macOS but Nix provides GNU sed/date; use GNU syntax (`sed -i "..."`, not BSD `sed -i ''`)
- [Platform foundation decisions](platform-foundation-decisions.md) — epic #64: single NixOS VM (Tier B ~$63/mo), Cloud SQL Postgres for Directus/Listmonk/FreeScout, domains, stack renamed prod, human-gated apply
- [Pulumi class-based pattern](pulumi-class-based-pattern.md) — author GCP resources as subclasses with secure defaults + grant methods; don't create resources until needed
- [Helpdesk tool selection](helpdesk-tool-selection.md) — FreeScout confirmed (SLA/reporting needed, collab-inbox limits hit); NO free Workspace: CSC pays Business Standard nonprofit $4.20/user (free tier lacks shared-drive access limits — don't suggest downgrade); mail source open: ~$50–70/mo licenses vs self-hosted mailboxes + Group front doors + SES
- [FreeScout mailbox options](freescout-mailbox-options.md) — DECIDED 2026-08-02: 1 Workspace seat, single shared inbox; outside assignees = free FreeScout users replying to notification emails (no login); a Google Group can't back a mailbox
- [Portal is a Google-auth POC](portal-public-no-auth.md) — cycsail.team portal (#82): static link site, NO app backend, gated by oauth2-proxy on all@; LIVE 2026-08-02 after boot-chain fixes; open item: cross-domain members need direct all@ membership or subgroup flags
- [Google group-membership API limits](google-group-membership-api-limits.md) — hasMember resolves nesting in-domain only; oauth2-proxy falls back to direct-only for cross-domain; checkTransitiveMembership needs Enterprise/CI Premium (CSC is Business Standard); DWD-via-ADC needs SA tokenCreator on itself
- [Clubspot API discovery (issue #90)](clubspot-api-discovery-issue-90.md) — Parse classes/functions for Events/Communication/E-signatures/Accounting found via dashboard network capture; `transactions` class = the GL journal, `qbo_sync_events` = daily QBO sync log

# CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project Overview

Isthmia is a collection of TypeScript packages for managing CYC Community Sailing Center operations, built as a pnpm monorepo. The system integrates with Clubspot (a sailing club management platform), Google Workspace, and deploys automated jobs to Google Cloud Platform.

## Development Environment

This project uses a **Nix flake** (with flake-parts) for reproducible development environments. All development commands should be run within the dev shell:

- Enter shell manually: `nix develop`
- Or use direnv to automatically load the environment: `direnv allow`

The dev shell provides:

- Node.js 22 with pnpm (via corepack)
- just (command runner)
- pulumi (infrastructure as code)
- google-cloud-sdk
- gam (Google Workspace admin tool)
- Pre-commit hooks via git-hooks.nix (treefmt for formatting, eslint for linting)

## Common Commands

Use `just` for all common tasks:

- `just` - List all available commands
- `just check` - Run formatting and linting checks
- `just build` - Build all packages using pnpm
- `just clean` - Clean all build artifacts
- `just ci` - Run full CI pipeline (check + build)
- `just deploy` - Deploy to GCP (requires authorization)

- `just test` - Run tests with vitest

### Package-specific Commands

Individual packages can be built using standard pnpm workspace commands:

- `pnpm run build` - Build all packages
- `pnpm run -r build` - Build all packages recursively
- `pnpm run clean` - Clean build artifacts

Each package uses TypeScript with `tsc --build` for compilation.

## Architecture

### Package Structure

The monorepo contains 7 packages organized as follows:

```
packages/
├── commodore/           # Shared CLI utilities (winston logging, commander.js helpers)
├── gsuite/              # Domain-agnostic wrappers around Google Workspace APIs
├── clubspot-sdk/        # TypeScript SDK for TheClubSpot API
├── admin-functions/     # Business logic for reports and data processing
├── todo-manager/        # CLI tool for syncing Todoist tasks
├── calendar-sync/       # CLI tool and library for syncing Google Calendar with Sheets
└── infrastructure/      # Pulumi-based GCP deployment configuration
```

### Dependency Graph

```
commodore (base utilities)
    ↑
    ├── clubspot-sdk (Parse SDK wrapper for TheClubSpot API)
    │       ↑
    │       ├── admin-functions (reports, participants, camps, sessions)
    │       └── todo-manager (Todoist integration)
    │
gsuite (Google Workspace API wrappers)
    ↑
    ├── admin-functions (uses spreadsheet abstractions)
    └── calendar-sync (uses Calendar & Spreadsheet clients)

infrastructure (deploys admin-functions as Cloud Run jobs)
```

### Key Components

**commodore**: Foundation package providing shared CLI and logging utilities. Uses commander-js for CLI parsing and winston for structured logging. Other CLI tools should depend on this for consistent logging and error handling.

**gsuite**: Domain-agnostic wrappers around Google Workspace APIs. Provides:

- `CalendarClient` - Google Calendar API wrapper with CRUD operations for events
- `SpreadsheetClient`, `Spreadsheet`, `Worksheet`, `Table` - Typed abstractions for Google Sheets with rate limiting
- `safeCall` - Rate-limited API call wrapper with exponential backoff retry
- Common utilities like `extractSpreadsheetId`

**clubspot-sdk**: SDK for interacting with TheClubSpot API (a Parse-based backend). The `Clubspot` class handles authentication and provides typed access to cloud functions and queries. Parse SDK is used under the hood with unsafe current user enabled for authentication state.

**admin-functions**: Contains business logic for generating reports about participants, registrations, camps, and sessions. Exports functions that can be invoked as Cloud Run jobs. Uses gsuite package for Google Sheets operations and Google Chat webhooks for notifications. The `runner.ts` module (`ReportRunner`) reads a config spreadsheet ("Reports" worksheet) and runs each enabled row; `reports.ts` defines the abstract `Report` base class and each report subclass registers in the `reports` map. This is the entry point deployed as the `run-reports-job` Cloud Run job.

**todo-manager**: CLI tool that syncs tasks from TheClubSpot (camp schedules) to Todoist. Uses the Doist Todoist API TypeScript client.

**calendar-sync**: CLI tool and library for syncing between Google Calendar and Google Spreadsheet. Can be used as a standalone library or invoked via CLI. Uses gsuite package for Calendar and Spreadsheet operations. Supports one-way sync in either direction with human-readable spreadsheet column headers.

**infrastructure**: Pulumi infrastructure-as-code that deploys admin-functions as containerized Cloud Run jobs on GCP. Creates:

- Docker images in GCP Artifact Registry
- Cloud Run jobs for running reports
- Service accounts with appropriate IAM roles
- Secret Manager secrets for Clubspot credentials

### Authentication

There are two independent auth systems. Do not confuse them.

#### Access policy (least privilege)

Root-level control of the GCP project and Google Workspace is reserved for the two Workspace
super-admin accounts, `master@cyccommunitysailing.org` and `commander@cyccommunitysailing.org`
(only `master@` exists today; `commander@` is planned as a second break-glass admin so root access
is never held by a single account). Those accounts are the only ones used for **configuration**
changes — org policy, project-root IAM, enabling services by hand, Workspace settings.

Individuals (e.g. `ungood@onetrue.name`) are granted only the narrower rights they need to test and
deploy: deploy permissions plus the ability to **impersonate service accounts** (never to log in as,
or hold the credentials of, the super-admin accounts). Day-to-day development and deploys therefore
run as your own account impersonating a service account — not as an admin. New principals default to
no access; grants are added deliberately in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`.

#### Google Cloud (Sheets, Calendar, deploys)

Google APIs use **two different credential types** for **two different purposes**:

| Purpose                                                                    | Credential                                | Command                                                     | Used by                                              |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Deploying (`just deploy`)                                                  | **User credentials**                      | `gcloud auth login` (→ `just auth-gcp`)                     | the `gcloud`, `pulumi`, and `docker` CLIs themselves |
| Running tools locally (`calendar-sync`, `admin-functions`, `todo-manager`) | **Application Default Credentials (ADC)** | `gcloud auth application-default login` (→ `just auth-adc`) | the Node.js `google-auth-library` inside the tools   |

**Which account:** Use your own account (`ungood@onetrue.name`) for `gcloud auth login`. It is granted deploy and impersonation rights in `packages/infrastructure/src/config.ts`. Do **not** log in as `master@cyccommunitysailing.org` for development.

**Which service account:** The deployed job runs as `report-runner@cyc-admin-scripts.iam.gserviceaccount.com`. To make local runs behave exactly like production (same permissions on the same spreadsheets), run tools by **impersonating that service account** via ADC — this is what `just auth-adc` does. This avoids "works locally but not in prod" surprises caused by your personal account having different sheet access.

> Note: the legacy `admin-scripts-runner@` service account still exists in GCP but is no longer used by any recipe. Its deletion is tracked separately in issue #58.

Alternatively, `GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS` can point at a service-account key file, but impersonation is preferred (no long-lived keys).

#### TheClubSpot (Parse backend)

Separate from Google. The system authenticates to TheClubSpot with a username/password:

1. Locally: supplied via `CLUBSPOT_EMAIL` / `CLUBSPOT_PASSWORD` env vars (or `-u`/`-p` flags — prefer env vars so the password is not visible in `ps`). In production: read from GCP Secret Manager secrets `clubspot-username` / `clubspot-password`.
2. Parse SDK is initialized with TheClubSpot's server URL and app ID.
3. User is looked up by email, then logged in with username/password.
4. Parse SDK's "unsafe current user" mode stores the session in memory (required for subsequent authenticated calls; see `Parse SDK Caveat` below).

## Deployment

Deployment to GCP requires:

1. GCP authentication as a deployer: `just auth-gcp` (`gcloud auth login`)
2. Access to the `cyc-admin-scripts` GCP project (granted in `config.ts`)
3. Run `just deploy` from repository root

Note: the image push no longer needs `gcloud auth configure-docker`. The Pulumi config in `run-reports-job.ts` authenticates the registry push with an OAuth2 access token minted from the running credentials (see the `registries` block), which also works when building through podman. `just deploy` starts a podman machine and points `DOCKER_HOST` at podman's socket.

The deployment:

- Builds all TypeScript packages
- Creates Docker images for admin-functions
- Pushes images to GCP Artifact Registry (us-west1)
- Updates Cloud Run jobs via Pulumi

## Testing

- Tests run with **vitest**: `just test` (or `vitest run`, or `vitest` for watch mode).
- Test files live at `packages/*/test/**/*.test.ts` (see `vitest.config.ts` `include`). Note this is a top-level `test/` directory per package, not co-located `.test.ts` files.
- Current coverage is thin: only `packages/gsuite/test/spreadsheet.test.ts` exists. It uses hand-rolled mock worksheets (no live Google API). New unit tests should follow that pattern — mock the external SDK boundary (Parse, google-spreadsheet, googleapis) and test pure logic.
- `just ci` runs `install → build → check → test`, matching the GitHub Actions `pr.yml` workflow.

## Code Style

- TypeScript with strict type checking (uses `@tsconfig/strictest`)
- ESLint with Prettier integration
- Pre-commit hooks enforce formatting and linting
- All packages use ESM (`"type": "module"`)
- Import paths use `.js` extension (TypeScript ESM convention)

## Important Technical Details

- **Parse SDK Caveat**: The clubspot-sdk enables `Parse.User.enableUnsafeCurrentUser()` to maintain authentication state. This is required for the Parse SDK to work correctly with subsequent API calls.
- **Engine Constraint**: `clubspot-sdk` declares `engines.node: ">= 20.8 < 21"` and `calendar-sync` declares `">= 20.8 < 23"`, but flake.nix (and the Docker base image) provide Node.js 22. The `< 21` bound on clubspot-sdk conflicts with the actual runtime; it is not currently enforced (no `engine-strict` in `.npmrc`) but should be widened to include 22 to avoid confusion.
- **Package Linking**: Some packages have self-references via `link:` in dependencies (e.g., `"@cyc-seattle/admin-functions": "link:"`) - these appear to be for local development
- **Security Overrides**: Root package.json includes pnpm overrides for security vulnerabilities in transitive dependencies

# Work an Issue

End-to-end workflow for taking an isthmia issue from open to merged. This repo uses a **PR flow — direct pushes to `main` are not allowed.** Everything goes through a feature branch and pull request.

**The automation never merges.** A human reviewer approves by merging the PR themselves — that manual merge _is_ the approval. The loop's job is to open the PR, keep CI green, respond to review feedback with revisions, and then clean up once the human has merged.

## Prerequisites

- Working tree is clean (`git status`). If there are unrelated uncommitted changes, ask the user how to handle them before branching.
- On `main` and up to date: `git switch main && git pull`.

## Workflow

### 1. Understand the issue

`gh issue view <N>` (add `--comments` if there's discussion). Restate the goal and the acceptance criteria in a sentence. If the issue is unclear or a duplicate, stop and flag it (see the `triage` skill).

### 2. Plan (only if the issue needs one)

Not every issue needs a plan. **Skip** for small, unambiguous changes (a one-line fix, a doc tweak, an obvious test). **Write a plan** when the issue is complex, ambiguous, architectural, touches multiple packages, or has more than one reasonable approach.

When a plan is warranted:

1. Write it as a comment on the issue — the intended approach, the files/packages affected, and any trade-offs or open questions: `gh issue comment <N> --body "..."` (prefix it clearly, e.g. `## Proposed plan`).
2. Mark the issue for review: `gh issue edit <N> --add-label "plan-review"`.
3. **Wait for a human contributor to approve or amend the plan.** Poll the issue (`gh issue view <N> --json labels,comments`). The human signals:
   - **Approved** — they remove the `plan-review` label (their manual go-ahead). Proceed to step 3.
   - **Changes requested** — they leave a comment. Revise the plan, post the updated version as a new comment, and keep waiting (label stays on).
4. Do **not** start implementing until the plan is approved. Use the same backed-off cadence as the PR loop (step 9) while waiting.

### 3. Create a branch

Branch off `main`, named `<type>/<issue#>-<slug>`, matching the issue's type label:

```sh
git switch -c fix/45-duplicate-events   # bug
git switch -c feat/47-auth-reconcile    # enhancement
git switch -c docs/21-readme-auth        # documentation
```

### 4. Write tests first (for bugs and testable logic)

Reproduce the bug with a failing test before fixing it. Tests live at `packages/<pkg>/test/**/*.test.ts` and run under vitest. Mock the external SDK boundary (Parse, google-spreadsheet, googleapis) — see `packages/gsuite/test/spreadsheet.test.ts` for the pattern. Run just the affected package's tests while iterating: `vitest run packages/<pkg>`.

### 5. Implement

Make the change. Match surrounding style: strict TypeScript, ESM with `.js` import extensions, imperative-capitalized commit subjects. Keep the diff scoped to the issue.

### 6. Verify locally

- Full gate (matches CI): `just ci` (install → build → check → test).
- Faster inner loop: `just check` (treefmt + eslint) and `just test`.
- For behavior that needs real Google/Clubspot access, verify with a manual run where feasible (see CLAUDE.md auth model) or clearly state in the PR what could only be tested via mocks.
- Pre-commit hooks (treefmt, eslint) run on commit — `just check` first avoids surprises.

### 7. Commit

Imperative, capitalized subject matching repo history (no conventional-commit prefixes). Reference the issue in the body:

```sh
git commit -m "Write new event ID back to sheet on recreate" -m "Fixes #45"
```

### 8. Push, open the PR, and request review

```sh
git push -u origin HEAD
gh pr create --fill --base main
```

- Ensure the PR body links the issue with a closing keyword (`Closes #45`) so the merge auto-closes it.
- Request review from the human reviewer(s) so the PR shows up in their queue: `gh pr edit <N> --add-reviewer <login>`.
- Post a short comment making the hand-off explicit: _"Ready for review. Merge it yourself when you're happy — that's the approval. I'll keep CI green and address any review comments."_
- Then enter the automated review loop (step 9).

### 9. Automated review loop (never merges)

Poll the PR on a cadence until the human merges it or closes it. Each cycle, gather state:

```sh
gh pr view <N> --json state,mergeStateStatus,statusCheckRollup,reviews,comments
```

Then act on it:

- **Merged by a human:** `state == "MERGED"` → go to step 10 (cleanup). This is the approval signal.
- **Closed without merging:** `state == "CLOSED"` → stop the loop and report; don't reopen or re-push.
- **CI red / failing checks:** get the failure (`gh run view <run-id> --log-failed`), fix on the branch, commit, push. To be woken when a run finishes rather than polling blindly, run `gh pr checks <N> --watch` in the background.
- **Changes requested or actionable review comments:** address each with commits on the same branch, push, and reply to the threads noting what changed. Don't force-push over review history unless asked. This is a _revision_ — the loop continues.
- **Green and waiting:** nothing to do — the PR is the human's to merge. Wait and re-check.

**Never run `gh pr merge`.** The automation keeps the PR healthy; the human presses merge.

**Cadence (use `ScheduleWakeup`):** while CI is actively running, check on a short interval (a few minutes). While idle waiting for the human to merge, back off to ~20–30 min so you don't burn cycles. Stop looping if the PR is merged or closed.

### 10. Clean up after the human merges

```sh
git switch main && git pull
git branch -d <branch>   # delete the local feature branch (remote branch is deleted at merge time or by GitHub)
```

Confirm the issue closed (the `Closes #N` keyword handles it). Report the merged PR and closed issue back to the user.

## Guardrails

- Never push directly to `main`. **Never merge PRs** — the human reviewer merges manually; that manual merge is the approval. The automation only opens the PR, keeps CI green, and addresses feedback.
- For issues that needed a plan (step 2), don't start implementing until the `plan-review` label is removed (plan approved).
- Keep one issue per branch/PR. If you discover unrelated problems, capture them as new issues (see the `capture` skill) rather than expanding scope.
- If CI keeps failing after a couple of honest fix attempts, or a review asks for something ambiguous, stop the loop and ask the user rather than guessing.

{"body":"## Problem

During the first real deploy of #97 (the people-hub/Directus rollout), Directus's own bootstrap
process ran migrations successfully (107 rows in `directus_migrations`) but never created the admin
user (0 rows in `directus_users`) or the default Administrator role/policy. `DirectusRole` /
`DirectusSchema` / `DirectusUser` (`packages/infrastructure/src/directus.ts`, `people-hub.ts`) all
authenticate as `ADMIN_EMAIL`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD` (the `directus-admin-bootstrap-password` secret) to do
their work via Directus's REST API — with no admin user existing, every one of them fails with a
bare `401 Invalid user credentials`, and `pulumi up` can't proceed at all.

Likely trigger: Directus's `bootstrap` command treats "has `directus_migrations` rows" as "already
installed" and skips admin-seeding on that basis — not "does an admin actually exist." In this
deploy, the substrate VM's `docker compose up -d` partially failed (the new `substrate-caddy-1`
container couldn't bind :80/:443 because the old `portal-caddy-1`/`portal-oauth2-proxy-1`
containers, from a completely separate never-torn-down compose project, were still holding them),
which plausibly interrupted Directus mid-bootstrap — after migrations completed, before
admin-seeding ran. Once that happens, no restart, no re-run of `directus bootstrap`, and no
`pulumi up` retry fixes it: the migrations table already has rows, so Directus always skips the
admin-seed step from then on. Recovery required manually running
`docker exec ... node cli.js users create ...` directly on the box — not reproducible, and not
something anyone should have to do again.

Two separate causes worth fixing:
1. `packages/substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml`'s project (`substrate`) collided on ports with the
   pre-existing `portal` project from before #97 — nothing tears down the old project when the
   compose project name changes.
2. The Pulumi automation (`directus.ts`'s `DirectusRole`/`DirectusSchema`/`DirectusUser`,
   `people-hub.ts`) has a hard, silent dependency on Directus's own opaque first-boot admin-seeding
   succeeding, with no verification, retry, or self-healing if it doesn't (for this reason or any
   other).

## Fix

- For (1): have the bootstrap script (`substrate-bootstrap.ts`) explicitly stop/remove containers
  from any other compose project sharing the host network ports before bringing up its own, or
  otherwise make the boot idempotent against stale prior projects.
- For (2): make the admin bootstrap self-healing rather than a silent prerequisite — e.g., have
  `directus.ts` check whether login as `ADMIN_EMAIL` succeeds, and if not, create the Administrator
  role/policy + admin user directly via the API (the same way `DirectusUser` already creates other
  users) before the rest of the automation runs. Add a regression test for the login-check/self-heal
  path if one can be written without a live Directus instance (a mocked HTTP layer, matching this
  package's existing test conventions where practical).

## Impact

Without this, any future fresh deploy (or anyone recovering a broken instance) can hit the exact
same dead end: full automation, `pulumi up` included, silently unable to proceed past a `401`, with

{"body":"## Problem

During the first real deploy of #97 (the people-hub/Directus rollout), Directus's own bootstrap
process ran migrations successfully (107 rows in `directus_migrations`) but never created the admin
user (0 rows in `directus_users`) or the default Administrator role/policy. `DirectusRole` /
`DirectusSchema` / `DirectusUser` (`packages/infrastructure/src/directus.ts`, `people-hub.ts`) all
authenticate as `ADMIN_EMAIL`/`ADMIN_PASSWORD` (the `directus-admin-bootstrap-password` secret) to do
their work via Directus's REST API — with no admin user existing, every one of them fails with a
bare `401 Invalid user credentials`, and `pulumi up` can't proceed at all.

Likely trigger: Directus's `bootstrap` command treats "has `directus_migrations` rows" as "already
installed" and skips admin-seeding on that basis — not "does an admin actually exist." In this
deploy, the substrate VM's `docker compose up -d` partially failed (the new `substrate-caddy-1`
container couldn't bind :80/:443 because the old `portal-caddy-1`/`portal-oauth2-proxy-1`
containers, from a completely separate never-torn-down compose project, were still holding them),
which plausibly interrupted Directus mid-bootstrap — after migrations completed, before
admin-seeding ran. Once that happens, no restart, no re-run of `directus bootstrap`, and no
`pulumi up` retry fixes it: the migrations table already has rows, so Directus always skips the
admin-seed step from then on. Recovery required manually running
`docker exec ... node cli.js users create ...` directly on the box — not reproducible, and not
something anyone should have to do again.

Two separate causes worth fixing:
1. `packages/substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml`'s project (`substrate`) collided on ports with the
   pre-existing `portal` project from before #97 — nothing tears down the old project when the
   compose project name changes.
2. The Pulumi automation (`directus.ts`'s `DirectusRole`/`DirectusSchema`/`DirectusUser`,
   `people-hub.ts`) has a hard, silent dependency on Directus's own opaque first-boot admin-seeding
   succeeding, with no verification, retry, or self-healing if it doesn't (for this reason or any
   other).

## Fix

- For (1): have the bootstrap script (`substrate-bootstrap.ts`) explicitly stop/remove containers
  from any other compose project sharing the host network ports before bringing up its own, or
  otherwise make the boot idempotent against stale prior projects.
- For (2): make the admin bootstrap self-healing rather than a silent prerequisite — e.g., have
  `directus.ts` check whether login as `ADMIN_EMAIL` succeeds, and if not, create the Administrator
  role/policy + admin user directly via the API (the same way `DirectusUser` already creates other
  users) before the rest of the automation runs. Add a regression test for the login-check/self-heal
  path if one can be written without a live Directus instance (a mocked HTTP layer, matching this
  package's existing test conventions where practical).

## Impact

Without this, any future fresh deploy (or anyone recovering a broken instance) can hit the exact
same dead end: full automation, `pulumi up` included, silently unable to proceed past a `401`, with
the only known fix being manual CLI surgery on the box.","comments":[],"labels":[{"id":"LA_kwDON4Gka88AAAAB5PiTuw","name":"bug","description":"Something isn't working","color":"d73a4a"},{"id":"LA_kwDON4Gka88AAAACqxFGvw","name":"P1","description":"High priority","color":"D93F0B"}],"state":"OPEN","title":"Directus first-boot admin creation isn't crash-safe or self-healing in deploy automation"}

29	// this package compiles to CommonJS) rather than the process cwd, so it works however Pulumi is
30	// invoked: <dir> -> infrastructure -> packages -> substrate.
31	const composeContent = readFileSync(resolve(__dirname, "../../substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml"), "utf8").trimEnd();
32	
33	const indent = (text: string, spaces: number): string =>
34	  text
35	    .split("\n")
36	    .map((line) => (line.length ? " ".repeat(spaces) + line : line))
37	    .join("\n");
38	
39	// Shell runs at first boot. `$VAR` / `$(...)` are shell (no `${` so template literals leave them
40	// alone); the interpolated `${...}` values are plain build-time strings.
41	function bootstrapScript(image: string, directusDbHost: string): string {
42	  return [
43	    "#!/bin/bash",
44	    "set -euo pipefail",
45	    "exec >> /var/log/substrate-bootstrap.log 2>&1",
46	    "mkdir -p /var/substrate",
47	    "META=http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1",
48	    `TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' "$META/instance/service-accounts/default/token" | grep -o '"access_token":"[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4)`,
49	    // The optional space after the colon matters: Secret Manager pretty-prints its JSON responses
50	    // (unlike the metadata server's compact token JSON above).
51	    "fetch_secret() {",
52	    `  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://secretmanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${projectId}/secrets/$1/versions/latest:access" | grep -o '"data": *"[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4 | base64 -d`,
53	    "}",
54	    "cat > /var/substrate/substrate.env <<EOF",
55	    `CADDY_IMAGE=${image}`,
56	    `SITE_DOMAIN=${internalDomain}`,
57	    `CRM_DOMAIN=${crmDomain}`,
58	    `OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_GROUP=${authGroup}`,
59	    `OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_ADMIN_EMAIL=${authAdminEmail}`,
60	    // One Google OAuth client, shared by oauth2-proxy (portal) and Directus's native OIDC (people
61	    // hub) — signing in once signs into both. See substrate.ts.
62	    "GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID=$(fetch_secret google-oauth-client-id)",
63	    "GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET=$(fetch_secret google-oauth-client-secret)",
64	    // oauth2-proxy only decodes URL-safe base64; translate the alphabet in case the stored value
65	    // was generated as standard base64 (same 32 bytes either way).
66	    "OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET=$(fetch_secret portal-oauth-cookie-secret | tr -- '+/' '-_')",
67	    `DIRECTUS_DB_HOST=${directusDbHost}`,
68	    `DIRECTUS_ADMIN_EMAIL=${directusAdminEmail}`,
69	    "DIRECTUS_KEY=$(fetch_secret directus-key)",
70	    "DIRECTUS_SECRET=$(fetch_secret directus-secret)",
71	    "DIRECTUS_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED directus-db-password)",
72	    "DIRECTUS_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(fetch_secret directus-admin-bootstrap-password)",
73	    // Optional: Directus runs on the Core tier if empty. See docs/manual-setup.md §6.
74	    "DIRECTUS_LICENSE_KEY=$(fetch_secret directus-license-key || true)",
75	    "EOF",
76	    // A fetch_secret failure inside the heredoc's command substitution doesn't trip `set -e`; it
77	    // just writes an empty value. Fail loudly instead of booting a service without credentials
78	    // (DIRECTUS_LICENSE_KEY excepted — optional, see above).
79	    "for key in GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET \\",
80	    "           DIRECTUS_KEY DIRECTUS_SECRET DIRECTUS_DB_PASSWORD DIRECTUS_ADMIN_PASSWORD; do",
81	    '  grep -q "^$key=.\\+" /var/substrate/substrate.env || { echo "$key is empty; secret fetch failed"; exit 1; }',
82	    "done",
83	    // COS mounts the root filesystem read-only, so docker's default config path (/root/.docker) is
84	    // unwritable; keep credentials under /var/substrate instead.
85	    "mkdir -p /var/substrate/.docker",
86	    "export DOCKER_CONFIG=/var/substrate/.docker",
87	    `docker login -u oauth2accesstoken -p "$TOKEN" https://${registryHost}`,
88	    // Prefer the compose v2 plugin, then the standalone binary. COS ships neither, so the last
89	    // resort runs compose out of the docker:cli image against the host socket, with the registry
90	    // credentials mounted where the containerized client expects them.
91	    "if docker compose version >/dev/null 2>&1; then DC='docker compose';",
92	    "elif command -v docker-compose >/dev/null 2>&1; then DC='docker-compose';",
93	    "else DC='docker run --rm -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v /var/substrate:/var/substrate -v /var/substrate/.docker:/root/.docker docker:cli compose'; fi",

102	    "",
103	    "write_files:",
104	    "  - path: /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml",

# The substrate VM's whole compose stack: every surface behind the one shared Caddy container,
# routed by hostname. Today that's the cycsail.team portal (gated by oauth2-proxy) and the people
# hub (Directus, its own native Google OIDC login — no oauth2-proxy needed for that surface). Secret
# values come from an env file written at boot from Secret Manager (see cloud-init in
# infrastructure/src/substrate-bootstrap.ts) — nothing sensitive lives in git.
services:
  caddy:
    image: ${CADDY_IMAGE}
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SITE_DOMAIN: ${SITE_DOMAIN}
      CRM_DOMAIN: ${CRM_DOMAIN}
    ports:
      - "80:80"
      - "443:443"
    volumes:
      - caddy_data:/data
      - caddy_config:/config
    depends_on:
      - oauth2-proxy
      - directus

  oauth2-proxy:
    image: quay.io/oauth2-proxy/oauth2-proxy:v7.6.0
    restart: unless-stopped
    command:
      - --http-address=0.0.0.0:4180
      - --reverse-proxy=true
      # Auth-only in front of Caddy: oauth2-proxy makes the allow/deny decision; Caddy serves.
      - --upstream=static://202
      - --provider=google
      - --redirect-url=https://${SITE_DOMAIN}/oauth2/callback
      - --cookie-domain=${SITE_DOMAIN}
      - --whitelist-domain=${SITE_DOMAIN}
      # Accept any Google account (personal Gmail included); the group check below is the real gate.
      - --email-domain=*
      # Authorization = membership in the all@ group (which nests staff@, volunteers@, …).
      - --google-group=${OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_GROUP}
      - --google-admin-email=${OAUTH2_PROXY_GOOGLE_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      # Use the VM's own service account (Application Default Credentials via the metadata server)
      # for the Directory API group lookup — no long-lived key file. The substrate SA must have
      # domain-wide delegation for admin.directory.group.readonly (see ../README.md).
      - --google-use-application-default-credentials=true
      - --set-xauthrequest=true
    environment:
      # Shared platform-wide Google OAuth client (substrate.ts) — SSO between this and Directus.
      OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_ID: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
      OAUTH2_PROXY_CLIENT_SECRET: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
      OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET: ${OAUTH2_PROXY_COOKIE_SECRET}

  # The people hub. Talks to its own database on the shared Cloud SQL instance over private IP
  # (no Cloud SQL Auth Proxy needed — the VM and Cloud SQL are on the same VPC).
  #
  # Directus 12+ (MSCL-licensed) gates custom/relational permission rules (the $CURRENT_USER-scoped
  # filters the Guardian policy depends on — see docs/people-hub-schema.md) behind a license; CYC
  # has one via Directus's Open Innovation Grant (nonprofit, well under the $5M revenue / 50
  # employee thresholds — see docs/manual-setup.md §6). LICENSE_KEY below is required for the
  # Guardian role to actually work, not just for this version number.
  directus:
    image: directus/directus:12.3.1
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      KEY: ${DIRECTUS_KEY}
      SECRET: ${DIRECTUS_SECRET}
      LICENSE_KEY: ${DIRECTUS_LICENSE_KEY}
      DB_CLIENT: pg
      DB_HOST: ${DIRECTUS_DB_HOST}
      DB_PORT: "5432"
      DB_DATABASE: directus
      DB_USER: directus
      DB_PASSWORD: ${DIRECTUS_DB_PASSWORD}
      ADMIN_EMAIL: ${DIRECTUS_ADMIN_EMAIL}
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: ${DIRECTUS_ADMIN_PASSWORD}
      PUBLIC_URL: https://${CRM_DOMAIN}
      # Native Google OIDC, same shared client as oauth2-proxy above — see
      # docs/manual-setup.md for the one-time OAuth client setup. No oauth2-proxy in front of this
      # surface; Directus enforces its own login + roles.
      AUTH_PROVIDERS: google
      AUTH_GOOGLE_DRIVER: openid
      AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID}
      AUTH_GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET: ${GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET}
      AUTH_GOOGLE_ISSUER_URL: https://accounts.google.com
      AUTH_GOOGLE_IDENTIFIER_KEY: email
      AUTH_GOOGLE_ALLOW_PUBLIC_REGISTRATION: "false"

volumes:
  caddy_data:
  caddy_config:

For directus.ts, mocking global fetch would let me simulate a Directus instance's login and creation flows, so I can test the role/user provider create methods and the eventual self-heal function. Now I'm sketching the self-healing fix, starting with a function to ensure the admin account is bootstrapped given the base URL and admin credentials.

But then I run into a real problem: if login fails there's no obvious way to create the admin role/user via the REST API without already having an admin token, since Directus's write endpoints all require auth and there's no exposed "create first admin" endpoint — that bootstrap normally happens internally at container startup via env vars, not through the API. So the self-heal approach as described may not actually be achievable purely through REST calls if no admin session exists yet, and I'm checking whether something like a public registration endpoint could work instead.

That's also unreliable, since re-running the CLI bootstrap doesn't fix it once the migrations table already has rows — Directus just skips the admin-seed step permanently after that. The known recovery method used a `docker exec` into the container to run the CLI directly, which isn't something a network-only dynamic resource provider can do unless we grant Pulumi SSH access to run commands on the VM, and that's a fragile pattern this file has deliberately avoided elsewhere.

A cleaner fix might be overriding the container's start command in the compose file to always run `directus bootstrap` before `directus start`, since bootstrap is supposed to be idempotent and separately checks for a missing admin user. But the issue explicitly states that simply restarting or re-running bootstrap doesn't fix it, so I need to dig into what Directus's bootstrap actually checks before relying on that approach.

Maybe the operator just restarted the container, which only runs `directus start` and skips bootstrap entirely, rather than literally re-executing `directus bootstrap`. That aligns with the issue's proposed fix: have directus.ts itself verify whether ADMIN_EMAIL can log in, and if not, create the Administrator role/policy and admin user directly via the API before the rest of the automation runs — though that would need an authenticated token first.

I'm stuck on how you'd get any token when zero admin users exist, since the roles/policies/users REST endpoints all require auth. Unless Directus has some special first-run allowance for the /users/register endpoint or similar, but I don't think that's the case — I need to check whether `directus bootstrap` itself is what creates that initial trust boundary.

Directus doesn't have that kind of unauthenticated bootstrap endpoint like Strapi does, so realistically the only path is SSH-exec into the container. Given the file's own comment noted they avoided an IAP-tunnel Command resource for a single GRANT statement due to fragility-for-one-statement, but here the payoff is much higher since it unblocks the whole admin chain, so a similar SSH-based approach might be worth it — unless there's a less invasive option via the Directus entrypoint script.

Given the uncertainty, I want to actually check Directus's source for how the bootstrap command handles admin creation, since I recall it roughly checks for and creates a default admin role/policy using fixed IDs if they don't already exist in the database within a transaction.

Thinking further, I don't believe Directus actually uses fixed role IDs anymore in v10+; instead the bootstrap only creates the admin role/policy/user if the users table is completely empty on a fresh install, rather than specifically verifying an admin exists — which lines up with the user's own theory that the bootstrap logic conflates "migrations table has rows" with "installation is already complete," rather than checking whether an admin account genuinely exists.

Since fixing Directus's internal bootstrap isn't something we control, our job is to make our own automation resilient regardless of the cause — verify login works and self-heal if it doesn't. I'm also considering whether the REST API offers any unauthenticated path to admin creation, but given that nearly all endpoints require auth except things like server info/ping/health, there doesn't appear to be a public users-creation route to exploit.

So without any existing credentials, self-healing purely via HTTP REST is impossible. The only viable paths are executing against the container itself over SSH via docker exec with the Directus CLI (mirroring the exact manual recovery process), or connecting directly to Postgres to insert rows — though that risks bypassing Directus's own password hashing and business logic. The CLI approach through a Pulumi dynamic resource over an IAP tunnel seems safest since it mirrors the proven manual fix exactly.

Since network.ts/compute.ts already establish IAP tunneling for SSH access, building a reusable SSH-based Pulumi Command resource seems like the intended pattern, even though I'd earlier avoided that overhead for a single Postgres GRANT statement — the payoff here is much higher since it covers the whole admin/role/schema chain used on every deploy. This does expand the scope of the fix considerably, requiring a new dynamic resource type that executes SSH commands over the IAP tunnel.

### 5.3 Access group — Workspace Admin console

- [x] `all@cyccommunitysailing.org` exists and nests the audience subgroups (`staff@`, `volunteers@`,
      …). Ensure the intended members are in it (including a test personal Gmail).

## 6. Directus / people hub (`crm.cycsail.team`)

Backing the people hub (see [docs/people-hub-schema.md](people-hub-schema.md)). No oauth2-proxy in
front of this surface — Directus authenticates directly via its own native Google OIDC (the shared
client from §5.1) and enforces roles/permissions server-side.

> ⚠️ **License note:** the relationship-based permission filters this data model depends on (a
> guardian reading only their own minor's record, e.g. the `Guardian` role's `$CURRENT_USER`-scoped
> rules) are gated behind a Directus license on v12+ (MSCL) — confirmed hands-on while building the
> schema (a fresh, unlicensed v12.3.1 instance rejected any permission with a `permissions` filter
> with `403 custom_permission_rules_enabled is a restricted resource`).
>
> CYC has a license via Directus's [Open Innovation Grant](https://directus.com/oig) (nonprofit,
> well under the $5M revenue / 50 employee thresholds — free, explicitly includes custom access
> policies, valid one year and renewable). `docker-compose.yml` is pinned to a current `12.x` with
> `LICENSE_KEY` wired in (§3, `directus-license-key`) — set that secret before first boot, and
> renew the grant/license annually.

Everything below is now `pulumi up` — the only genuinely irreducible manual step left is the one
Postgres `GRANT` in §6.1 (it needs a live SQL connection; nothing that runs `pulumi up` has a
network path to Cloud SQL's private IP today). No more `directus schema apply` CLI, no more
first-boot-admin-then-create-my-account dance, no more secret values to invent — `directus-key`,
`directus-secret`, `directus-db-password`, `directus-admin-bootstrap-password`, and
`portal-oauth-cookie-secret` are all Pulumi-generated now (see `randomSecret` in `secret.ts`),
nothing to fill in for them in §3.

### 6.1 Database role — Cloud SQL

Pulumi creates the `directus` Postgres role itself (`postgres.user()` in `database.ts`, via the
Cloud SQL Admin API — no network path to the instance needed for that part) with the generated
`directus-db-password` value. What Pulumi **can't** do: grant that role privileges on the
`directus` database — Postgres 16's tightened default (no public `CREATE` on a fresh database's
`public` schema) means that needs a live SQL connection, and Cloud SQL here is private-IP-only with
no network path from wherever `pulumi up` runs. One remaining manual step:

- [ ] Connect to the `substrate` Cloud SQL instance (`gcloud sql connect substrate --user=postgres`,
      or via a bastion/IAP tunnel) and run:
      `sql
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA public TO directus;
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE directus TO directus;
`
      (Deliberately not automated with an IAP-tunnel-in-a-Pulumi-resource for one `GRANT` — the
      fragility didn't seem worth it for something this narrow. Say so if that trade-off should go
      the other way.)

### 6.2 Schema, roles, and the first Staff account — all `pulumi up`

`infrastructure/src/people-hub.ts` applies the committed
[`packages/people-hub/schema.yaml`](../packages/people-hub/schema.yaml) snapshot
(`DirectusSchema`, via Directus's own `/schema/diff` + `/schema/apply` REST endpoints — going
through the running server's API instead of the CLI also means no restart-for-stale-cache gotcha),
creates the Staff/Coach/Guardian roles (`DirectusRole`), and provisions `ungood@onetrue.name` as a
Staff user via Google OIDC (`DirectusUser` — no password; signing in with that Google account just
works, no bootstrap-admin dance).

- [ ] `pulumi up`. Needs `directus-admin-bootstrap-password` to already have a value (Pulumi
      generates it — see above, nothing to do) and Directus to already be reachable at
      `https://crm.cycsail.team` — these resources retry for a few minutes if it isn't yet, but
      won't wait forever. On a truly fresh deploy this is often the _second_ `pulumi up` (first:
      secrets/DB/DNS containers + the VM; you do §6.1's `GRANT` and confirm the VM picked up the
      compose stack; second: this).
- [ ] Provisioning additional staff this way (rather than through the Directus UI) is a reasonable
      next step once there's an actual list of who needs access — add more `DirectusUser` resources
      to `people-hub.ts`.

---

## When you add a new manual step

If you introduce infrastructure that needs an out-of-band action, add it here (and cross-link from
the relevant package README), so this stays the single source of truth for "things I had to do by
hand."

content.content:
# Manual setup steps

Most of this platform is infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi, in `packages/infrastructure`). A handful of
steps **cannot** be — they live in Google consoles, the Workspace Admin console, or the domain
registrar, or they involve secret _values_ that must never enter git. This doc is the running record
of every such out-of-band step, so setting up a fresh environment (or recovering one) doesn't rely
on memory.

Legend: `[ ]` = to do for a new setup, `[x]` = done for the current production setup (as of this doc).

> Why these can't be code: OAuth "Web application" clients and the **External** consent screen have
> no Terraform/Pulumi resource; domain-wide delegation and Workspace settings live in the Admin
> console and would require super-admin credentials that our access policy deliberately keeps out of
> automation (see [CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md) → Access policy); registrar delegation is at the domain
> registrar; and external credentials (OAuth secrets, third-party logins) are set out of band by
> design — Pulumi declares only the container for those. Internal keys/passwords with no meaningful
> human choice are the exception: Pulumi generates and manages those values directly (see §3).

---

## 1. Project & organization bootstrap (super-admin)

Done as a Workspace **super-admin** (`master@cyccommunitysailing.org`). Reserved to super-admins per
the access policy — not day-to-day deploy identities.

- [x] GCP project `cyc-admin-scripts` created under the org.
- [x] Org policy / project-root IAM as needed.
- [ ] Any Google API that must be enabled by hand (most are enabled in code via the `enableService`
      helper; enable by hand only if a chicken-and-egg case appears).

## Summary

Root-cause fix for #99: the substrate compose stack collided on host ports 80/443 with the
pre-substrate-rename `portal` compose project, which was never torn down. That collision plausibly
interrupted Directus mid-bootstrap during the #97 deploy, before it seeded the admin user/role —
Directus's own install-check is gated on migrations having run, not on an admin actually existing, so
once that happens no restart/retry fixes it (confirmed by reproducing the exact scenario against a
local Directus container — see commit message).

Per discussion on the issue: no self-healing/auto-repair. I initially proposed a self-heal that
recreates the admin via Directus's REST API, but verified locally that's not actually possible (every
write endpoint 403s with zero users — Directus has no unauthenticated bootstrap escape hatch). Since
this looks like a one-time first-deploy bug, the agreed call is to fix the actual trigger (this PR)
and, separately, wipe the currently-broken live Directus state and redeploy clean — not build new
SSH-exec automation for something the trigger fix should prevent from recurring.

Also includes an already-in-progress, independent fix: `getSecretVersionOutput` for the admin
bootstrap password had no `dependsOn` on the secret's own `SecretVersion` write, so the read had no
ordering guarantee against it on a fresh deploy.

## Changes

- `substrate-bootstrap.ts`: cloud-init now removes any running container whose
  `com.docker.compose.project` label isn't this project's own before pulling/starting the stack.
- Extracted the cloud-init string-templating into a new pulumi-free `substrate-bootstrap-script.ts`
  so it's unit testable (the original file's top-level pulumi/GCP resource construction makes it
  unimportable from a plain vitest test).
- `secret.ts` / `people-hub.ts`: thread the `SecretVersion` resource through `randomSecret`'s return
  value and `dependsOn` it when reading the admin bootstrap password back.

## Test plan

- [x] `just ci` (build, format/lint, vitest) passes.
- [x] New unit test (`substrate-bootstrap-script.test.ts`) covers the cleanup-ordering and
      project-name-scoping logic.
- [x] Manually verified the actual cleanup shell logic against real containers on a local Docker
      network (a stale differently-labeled container holding a port gets removed; same-project and
      unrelated containers don't) — not something CI can exercise since it needs a real Docker
      daemon and simulated stale state.
- [x] Manually reproduced the original failure against a local `directus/directus:12.3.1` +
      Postgres container (wiped admin/role/policy rows while leaving migrations intact, restarted —
      confirmed the permanent 401) to confirm the root-cause hypothesis before fixing it.

Closes #99
EOF

# Capture an Issue

Turn a problem — from the current conversation or the user's description — into a well-formed GitHub issue in `cyc-seattle/isthmia`.

## Steps

1. **Gather the problem.** Pull details from the conversation or ask the user. A good issue needs: what's wrong or wanted, where in the code (`path:line`), and why it matters.
2. **Check for duplicates first.** `gh issue list --state open --limit 100 --json number,title,labels`. If it overlaps an existing issue, tell the user and offer to comment on / rescope that one instead of filing a new duplicate.
3. **Pick a type label:** `bug`, `enhancement`, `documentation`, or `docker`.
4. **Assign a priority label** using the rubric below.
5. **Write the body** using the template below. Reference concrete files as `path:line`.
6. **Create it:** `gh issue create --title "<imperative title>" --label "<type>,<priority>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"`
7. **Report** the issue number and URL back to the user.

## Priority rubric (P0–P3)

- **P0 — Critical:** data integrity/corruption, production broken, or a security-critical hole. Work starts immediately.
- **P1 — High:** a significant bug or friction the user hits regularly, with no safe workaround (e.g. auth/tooling breakage).
- **P2 — Medium:** a real improvement or a bug with a workaround (added tests, hardening, moderate bugs).
- **P3 — Low:** cleanup, docs, polish, low-risk nice-to-haves.

## Body template

Keep it tight. Use `## Problem` always; then `## Fix` (bugs) or `## Proposed changes` / `## Scope` (enhancements); add `## Impact` when the "why" isn't obvious.

```markdown
## Problem

<what's wrong/wanted, with `path:line` references and a code snippet if useful>

## Fix

<concrete change; mention adding a regression test for bugs>

## Impact

<why it matters — omit if self-evident>
```

## Conventions

- **Title:** short, imperative, no priority prefix (priority lives in the label). e.g. "safeCall retries non-retryable errors with a 60s delay".
- Labels already exist: `P0`–`P3`, `bug`, `enhancement`, `documentation`, `docker`. Don't invent new ones without asking.
- For bugs, always note that the fix should include a regression test — tests live in `packages/*/test/**/*.test.ts`.
- Cross-link related issues with `#N` and note dependencies ("land #47 first").

## Problem

`pulumi up` fails applying the people hub's Directus schema:

```
POST /schema/diff -> 400: {"errors":[{"message":"Invalid payload. Provided snapshot's directus
version 11.17.4 does not match the current instance's version 12.3.1. You can bypass this check by
passing the \"force\" query parameter.", ...}]}
```

`packages/people-hub/schema.yaml:1-2` declares:

```yaml
version: 1
directus: 11.17.4
```

but `packages/substrate/deploy/docker-compose.yml` pins `directus/directus:12.3.1`. `DirectusSchema`
(`packages/infrastructure/src/directus.ts`'s `applySchema`, via `POST /schema/diff` +
`POST /schema/apply`) doesn't pass Directus's `force` query parameter, so the version check always
rejects it. This blocks `people-hub-schema` from ever being created — and everything that
`dependsOn` it (`people-hub-staff`/`-coach`/`-guardian` roles, `people-hub-staff-ungood`) with it.

Surfaced 2026-09-09 during the first `pulumi up` to ever get past #99's admin-bootstrap fix — this
is the very next step in the same dependency chain, so it's effectively still blocking the initial
people-hub deploy from completing.

## Fix

Most likely just a stale metadata field: `docs/manual-setup.md` §6 notes the schema's permission
filters (the license-gated `$CURRENT_USER` relational rules) were already hand-tested against a real
Directus 12.3.1 instance, so the schema content itself is very likely already compatible — the
`directus: 11.17.4` line looks like it was never updated after the compose file was later pinned to
12.3.1 for the license feature. Bump `packages/people-hub/schema.yaml`'s `directus:` field to
`12.3.1` and re-verify the diff/apply succeeds against a real 12.3.1 instance (not just blindly pass
`force` in `applySchema` — that would permanently mask any future real incompatibility instead of
fixing this one).

Add a regression test if practical (mock `fetch` around `applySchema`/`directusSchemaProvider` to
assert the version in the schema payload is checked/kept in sync, or at least that a version
mismatch surfaces clearly) — see existing test conventions in `packages/gsuite/test/`.

## Impact

Blocks the people hub's very first successful deploy — the schema/roles/first-staff-user resources
can never be created until this is fixed, regardless of #99 being fixed.
EOF

cat > /tmp/pr-101-body.md << 'EOF'
## Summary

Fixes #101: `packages/people-hub/schema.yaml` recorded `directus: 11.17.4`, but the compose stack
pins `directus/directus:12.3.1` (for the Open Innovation Grant license features). Directus's
`/schema/diff` rejects any snapshot whose recorded version doesn't match the running instance, so
this blocked `DirectusSchema` — and everything downstream of it (`people-hub-staff`/`-coach`/
`-guardian` roles, `people-hub-staff-ungood`) — from ever being created. Surfaced tonight as the very
next blocker after #99's admin-bootstrap fix got past the first one.

## Change

One line: bump the recorded version to `12.3.1`. Not passing Directus's `force` bypass instead —
that would permanently mask any future real incompatibility rather than fixing this one, and the
mismatch here really was just a stale field.

## Test plan

- [x] `just ci` passes.
- [x] Verified against a live local `directus/directus:12.3.1` container: replayed the exact
      `/schema/diff` → `/schema/apply` round trip `directus.ts`'s `applySchema` does. Before the
      bump: `400` (the reported version-mismatch error). After: `200` on diff, `204` on apply, and
      the collections (`people`, `registrations`, etc.) actually exist afterward — confirms the
      schema content itself was already 12.3.1-compatible, only the version tag was stale.
- Note: a re-diff after applying isn't perfectly empty — it reports a couple of newer per-collection
  meta keys (`autosave_revision_interval`, `status`) that 12.x adds and the older-authored snapshot
  doesn't declare. Cosmetic/non-blocking (no errors, nothing gets deleted), not something this PR
  needs to chase down.

Closes #101
EOF

## Summary

Directus is the data layer's admin screen (Layer 2's engine), not a customer-facing CRM surface —
requested rename to reflect that: `crm.<domain>` -> `directus.<domain>`.

## Changes

- DNS record, Directus's own `baseUrl`, and the compose stack's env var (`CRM_DOMAIN` ->
  `DIRECTUS_DOMAIN`) all renamed.
- `substrate-bootstrap.ts`'s internal `crmDomain` identifier -> `directusDomain`.
- Caddyfile's domain matcher + comments updated to match.
- Docs (`manual-setup.md`, `architecture.md`) and `substrate/README.md` updated wherever they
  referenced the literal `crm.cycsail.team` / `crm.*` subdomain.

## Follow-up (not in this PR)

Once this deploys, the Google OAuth client's authorized redirect URIs needs
`https://directus.cycsail.team/auth/login/google/callback` added (console-only setting, no Pulumi
resource for it — see `docs/manual-setup.md` §5).

## Test plan

- [x] `just ci` passes.
- [x] Grepped the whole repo for `crm.` after the change — no leftover references.

Closes nothing (no issue filed — direct request); this is unrelated to #99/#101/#100/#102.
EOF

21	// The people hub's subdomain and its first-boot Directus superadmin account.

30	// invoked: <dir> -> infrastructure -> packages -> substrate.

35	    .split("\n")
36	    .map((line) => (line.length ? " ".repeat(spaces) + line : line))

41	function bootstrapScript(image: string, directusDbHost: string): string {
42	  return [
43	    "#!/bin/bash",
44	    "set -euo pipefail",

46	    "mkdir -p /var/substrate",
47	    "META=http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1",
48	    `TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Metadata-Flavor: Google' "$META/instance/service-accounts/default/token" | grep -o '"access_token":"[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4)`,
49	    // The optional space after the colon matters: Secret Manager pretty-prints its JSON responses
50	    // (unlike the metadata server's compact token JSON above).

52	    `  curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "https://secretmanager.googleapis.com/v1/projects/${projectId}/secrets/$1/versions/latest:access" | grep -o '"data": *"[^"]*"' | cut -d'"' -f4 | base64 -d`,

55	    `CADDY_IMAGE=${image}`,
56	    `SITE_DOMAIN=${internalDomain}`,
57	    `CRM_DOMAIN=${crmDomain}`,

70	    "DIRECTUS_SECRET=$(fetch_secret directus-secret)",
71	    "DIRECTUS_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED directus-db-password)",
72	    "DIRECTUS_ADMIN_PASSWORD=$(fetch_secret directus-admin-bootstrap-password)",

94	    "$DC --project-directory /var/substrate --env-file /var/substrate/substrate.env -f /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml pull",
95	    "$DC --project-directory /var/substrate --env-file /var/substrate/substrate.env -f /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml up -d",
96	  ].join("\n");
97	}

99	function cloudConfig(image: string, directusDbHost: string): string {
100	  return [
101	    "#cloud-config",
102	    "",
103	    "write_files:",
104	    "  - path: /var/substrate/docker-compose.yml",
105	    '    permissions: "0644"',
106	    "    content: |",
107	    indent(composeContent, 6),
108	    "  - path: /var/substrate/bootstrap.sh",
109	    '    permissions: "0755"',
110	    "    content: |",
111	    indent(bootstrapScript(image, directusDbHost), 6),
112	    "",
113	    "runcmd:",
114	    "  - ['/bin/bash', '/var/substrate/bootstrap.sh']",

121	  .all([imageUrl, postgres.privateIpAddress])
122	  .apply(([image, directusDbHost]) => cloudConfig(image, directusDbHost));
